title: Rest
hook: sleep as practice; the mantra at bedtime

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ekadashi, the eleventh day, twice a month. Your line was a rhythm. Did you find the moon, or the next Ekadashi? Day one hundred and thirty-one.

Look at this week. It started with the body as a temple: this is where you live. Then a bow to the sun. A vow, and chosen hunger. Sattvic food, eaten quiet. Prasad, the sweet that returns. And Ekadashi, a rhythm set by the moon. Six days of caring for the building. But the thing the body asks for most, every single night, is the thing most of us treat as a leftover. We sleep when we've finished scrolling. We sleep when we collapse. What if sleep weren't the end of the day's practice, but part of it? Today: rest.
screen: `A WEEK OF CARING FOR THE BUILDING.` → `SLEEP, TREATED AS A LEFTOVER.` → `TODAY: REST.`

segments.voice: One of the shortest Upanishads, the Mandukya, takes sleep very seriously. It describes three states everyone moves through every day. Waking, when you're turned outward to the world. Dreaming, when you're turned inward, making worlds of your own. And deep, dreamless sleep, when there's no wanting and no picture at all, and the text calls that state full of peace, even bliss. Then it points to a fourth, beyond all three, the steady awareness that is there through them all. And it maps them onto the sound you learned on day two. Om is really three sounds, A, U and M: waking, dreaming, deep sleep. And the silence after the M is the fourth. So every night, you move through Om without saying it. That changes what bedtime can be. Many Hindus fall asleep with a name or a mantra: Ram, or Krishna, or Om namah shivaya, said quietly until it fades. Some elders connect it to an idea in the Gita, that what a person remembers at the very end shapes where they go next, and they practice the idea small, every night: let the last thing in the mind be something good. And the Mandukya's quiet point is that deep sleep isn't nothing. It's rest so complete that even the self stops needing to hold itself up. You can't force it. You can only put things down so it can come. Rest isn't time off from the practice. It's the practice, lying down.
screen: `WAKING, DREAMING, DEEP SLEEP.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE AFTER.` · `A NAME AS THE LAST THING.` · `REST IS THE PRACTICE, LYING DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tonight, try this at bedtime; for now, try it where you are. Put your phone face down, out of reach. Let your body get heavy, the way it does just before sleep. Breathe in, and breathe out long and slow. Now, silently or in a whisper, if you'd like: Om. Feel the A open, the U round, the M hum, and then the silence. Twice more. If you have a name or mantra of your own, let it be the last thing. Then just rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Rest. Sleep as part of the practice: waking, dreaming and deep sleep, A, U and M, with a name as the last thing before the quiet. Today's word.
Your line: put it down. Tonight, put the phone down first, then let a name or Om be the last thing in your mind. That's the week. Tomorrow we walk into a temple. Day one hundred and thirty-one.

howItsDone: Many Hindus end the day by saying a name of God or a short mantra before sleep, and the Mandukya Upanishad's teaching on waking, dreaming, deep sleep and the fourth state is often linked to the three sounds of Om and the silence after it.

what a scholar hears: the Mandukya Upanishad names waking (vaishvanara), dreaming (taijasa) and deep sleep (prajna) and a fourth (turiya), mapping them onto A, U, M and the silence; Gita 8.5–6 is about remembrance at the moment of death, applied by some to sleep.
